relevance_reason: Reports a patient with a de novo truncating FBRSL1 variant and a syndromic NDD, with zebrafish functional modeling, directly relevant to CIDFS.

findings.statement: Xu et al. (2026) described a patient with neurodevelopmental delay, epilepsy, congenital heart disease, and facial dysmorphism.
quotes: We identified a de novo FBRSL1 variant p.Ala128Cysfs*5 in a patient with neurodevelopmental delay, epilepsy, congenital heart disease, and facial dysmorphism.

findings.statement: In a patient with neurodevelopmental delay, epilepsy, congenital heart disease, and facial dysmorphism, Xu et al. (2026) identified a de novo truncating variant in the FBRSL1 gene, p.Ala128Cysfs*5, by whole-exome sequencing.
quotes: Whole-exome sequencing was conducted to identify possible pathogenic variants.
We identified a de novo FBRSL1 variant p.Ala128Cysfs*5 in a patient with neurodevelopmental delay, epilepsy, congenital heart disease, and facial dysmorphism.

findings.statement: Xu et al. (2026) analyzed 4 patients with FBRSL1 variants and described an emerging syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by microcephaly, global developmental delay, autism, facial dysmorphism, and skeletal contractures.
quotes: Further analysis of four patients with FBRSL1 variants revealed an emerging syndromic NDD, characterized by microcephaly, global developmental delay, autism, facial dysmorphism, and skeletal contractures.

findings.statement: Xu et al. (2026) found that fbrsl1 knockdown in zebrafish recapitulated neurodevelopmental abnormalities, epileptiform discharges, and cardiac dysfunction, consistent with the patient's phenotype.
quotes: Zebrafish knockdown models recapitulated neurodevelopmental abnormalities, epileptiform discharges, and cardiac dysfunction, consistent with the patient's phenotypes.

findings.statement: Xu et al. (2026) found that FBRSL1 is highly expressed in the developing brain and heart, and single-cell RNA sequencing showed high expression in neural progenitors of 1-month-old organoids, suggesting a vital role in neurodevelopment.
quotes: FBRSL1 is highly expressed in the developing brain and heart, potentially explaining its multisystem phenotypes.
Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed a high expression of FBRSL1 in neural progenitors of 1-month-old organoids, suggesting its vital role in neurodevelopment.

relevance_reason: Case report of an additional patient with a de novo truncating FBRSL1 variant and the syndromic phenotype described by Ufartes et al. (2020), with clinical, molecular, methylation and management data.

findings.statement: Bukvic et al. (2024) reported a girl, the third child of healthy nonconsanguineous Italian parents (father 46, mother 38 years old at her birth), with threatened miscarriage and poor fetal movements in pregnancy. At term she had low birth weight (2860 g) and length below the 3rd centile, neonatal feeding difficulties due to weak sucking, postnatal growth retardation, bilateral contractures of hands and fingers, bilateral congenital hip dislocation, and irregular bone growth fronts of the long bones; she was initially diagnosed with arthrogryposis multiplex congenita at 4 months of age.
quotes: The proband was the third child born of a healthy non-consanguineous Italian couple (see pedigree—Figure 1).

Her birth weight was 2860 g (<10th centile), length 39.5 cm (<3rd centile), head circumference 34 cm (<50th centile). She had neonatal feeding difficulties, due to weak sucking, and postnatal growth retardation.
bilateral contractures on hands and fingers; bilateral congenital dislocation of the hip; femurs, radius and ulnas manifested distal irregularities of bone growth front

phenotypes.text: neonatal feeding difficulties due to weak sucking
bilateral contractures of hands and fingers
irregular bone growth fronts of long bones

findings.statement: Bukvic et al. (2024) noted that the patient had global developmental delay (head control at 7 months, sitting at 14 months, walking unsupported at 46 months), no active speech and severe intellectual disability at 48 months (developmental quotient 22), and motor stereotypies without autism spectrum disorder. At 48 months she had short stature, low weight, microcephaly, and facial dysmorphism including flat occiput, frontal bossing, midface hypoplasia, short philtrum, micrognathia, and microstomia with 'whistling mouth'; later examination noted small forehead, bitemporal narrowing, sunken eyes, broad nasal bridge, unusual ears, and thick lips. She also had mild scoliosis, distal limb hypertonia with supinated varus feet, wide-based gait, and cerebral palsy/spasticity; hearing and heart were normal, and brain and spinal MRI at 2 months and 4 years and metabolic studies were normal.
quotes: At 48 months of age, she did not develop active speech, and she showed severe intellectual disability (her developmental quotient was 22 as tested with Griffiths Mental Development Scales).

she showed also microcephaly (head circumference was 45.3 cm, −2.68 SD bellow 3rd centile) and facial dysmorphism (flat back of the head, frontal bossing, mid-face hypoplasia, short philtrum, micrognathia, and microstomia with “whistling mouth” (Figure 2).
Audiology assessment was normal, and no heart defect was found.

findings.statement: Bukvic et al. (2024) reported that at 46 months of age the patient developed epilepsy with daily drop tonic seizures and later myoclonic absences; ictal EEG showed a high-voltage slow wave followed by voltage attenuation and interictal EEG showed frontocentral spikes and spike-and-wave complexes and 2-Hz diffuse spike-and-wave complexes. Epilepsy, stereotypies, hip dislocation, and mastication problems were noted as features not previously reported in FBRSL1 patients, whereas respiratory insufficiency, cleft palate, heart defects, and hearing impairment reported by Ufartes et al. (2020) were absent.
quotes: At the age of 46 months, epileptic attacks were registered with daily drop tonic seizures, lasting a few seconds, single and in runs, in most cases during wakefulness and without fall.

Interictal EEG showed abnormal sleep architecture and the presence of frequent spikes and spike-and-wave complexes on the bilateral fronto-central regions, the same as midline region, and brief 2 Hz diffuse spike-and-wave complexes (Figure 3B).

However, our patient reported clinical characteristics basically comparable with those of the three patients reported by Ufartes et al. (2020), and at the age of 46 months manifested epileptic attacks.

findings.statement: In the Italian girl, Bukvic et al. (2024) identified by trio clinical exome sequencing a de novo heterozygous 1-bp duplication in exon 2 of the FBRSL1 gene (c.371dupC, NM_001142641.2), causing a frameshift and premature stop codon (p.Cys125Leufs*7) predicted to yield a 131-amino acid protein instead of 1045 residues; the variant was confirmed by Sanger sequencing and absent from the parents. No other variants explaining the phenotype were found.
quotes: Trio clinical exome sequencing (CES) showed in exon 2 of the FBRSL1gene a de novo heterozygous variant, duplication: c.371dupC (NM_001142641.2), causing frameshift and leading to a premature stop codon (p.Cys125Leufs*7)—(Figure 4).
No additional de novo variants or other variants explaining the child’s symptoms were detected by the exome sequencing.

findings.statement: Bukvic et al. (2024) found by SNP array in the patient a paternally inherited approximately 530-kb duplication at 7p11.2 and two maternally inherited duplications at 16p13.11 (about 470 kb and 1.1 Mb), all classified as variants of uncertain significance; STITCH analysis found no interactions attributable to these duplications that could be linked to the phenotype.
quotes: SNP array analysis had been performed previously with subsequently reported results: one paternal duplication, ~530 Kb in 7p11.2 (56118293–56639964), and two maternal duplications: the first of ~470 Kb in 16p13.11 (14866284–15328800) and a second one of ~1.1 Mb in 16 p13.11 (15417031–16529801).
All three microduplications (2 mat and 1 pat, respectively) were considered as variants of uncertain significance (VUS).

findings.statement: Bukvic et al. (2024) found that genome-wide DNA methylation analysis (EpiSign) of the patient's peripheral blood showed a profile similar to controls for all episignatures tested, including the PRC2 episignature (MVP score of zero); FBRSL1 or PRC1.5 episignatures are undefined.
quotes: EpiSign assessment of the patient revealed a genome-wide DNA methylation profile that aligned with negative controls across all episignatures evaluated, including the one associated with the polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2), as indicated by an MVP score of zero.

findings.statement: Bukvic et al. (2024) used in silico modeling of the truncated 131-residue FBRSL1 protein and predicted a self-binding domain (residues 81 to 93) and 2 nuclear localization signals; they hypothesized that the truncated protein could localize to the nucleus and inactivate wildtype FBRSL1, suggesting a possible dominant-negative effect.
quotes: The truncated version found in the patient, which shows two nuclear localization signals, could localize in the nucleus, and thanks to the self-binding domain formed by amino acid residues 81–93, interact with the wild-type isoforms of FBRSL1, inactivating them. This could confer a possible negative dominance effect on the mutation in our case.

findings.statement: Bukvic et al. (2024) reported that the patient's seizures initially responded well to valproic acid but relapsed months later, with better but incomplete control after addition of ethosuximide and rufinamide. A percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy was placed at 6 years for feeding difficulties and poor weight gain, and with multidisciplinary rehabilitation including augmentative and alternative communication she became able to sit and stand independently, walk with minimal support, and communicate basic needs.
quotes: Valproic acid (VPA) was administered early with immediately good control of seizures, but months later, the patient underwent a relapse with daily drop tonic seizures and myoclonic absences, so ethosuximide and rufinamide were added to valproic acid with better but not complete control.
at the age of 6 years, a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) procedure for enteral feeding was performed due to well-known feeding difficulties and poor weight gain.

The patient achieved most of her development milestones and is now able to sit independently, stand independently, reach, grasp, release and manipulate objects of interest with her upper limbs and hands, and walk with minimal support.

relevance_reason: This is a review. It summarizes the three FBRSL1 patients previously reported by Ufartes et al. (2020) and compares their syndrome with AUTS2 syndrome using the AUTS2 severity scoring features. It also summarizes the Xenopus model and FBRSL1 isoform data. It reports no new patients.

findings.statement: Pauli et al. (2021) reviewed 3 unrelated children with truncating FBRSL1 variants. In the newborn period they had breathing failure needing ventilation and feeding difficulties. Later they showed intellectual disability with no active speech, postnatal microcephaly, growth retardation and contractures. Two of the 3 had cleft palate and heart defects (atrial septal defect with patent ductus arteriosus in one, atrial and ventricular septal defects in the other); 1 had asplenia and 1 had anal atresia. The 2 more severely affected children were born with marked skin creases that disappeared during the first year of life.
quotes: The patients presented with respiratory insufficiency and feeding difficulties in the neonatal period. During infancy, intellectual disability, no active speech, postnatal microcephaly, growth retardation and contractures became apparent.

In addition, two of the three patients showed cleft palate and heart defects (one with atrial septal defect and persistent ductus arteriosus, one with atrial septal defect and ventricular septal defect). In one patient asplenia and in another patient anal atresia were observed.

the two more severely affected patients were born with pronounced congenital skin creases at the back, the arms, and legs. During the first year of life the skin creases became less pronounced and disappeared

findings.statement: Pauli et al. (2021) compared the 3 FBRSL1 patients with AUTS2 syndrome using the features of the AUTS2 syndrome severity scoring system. All 3 had short stature, microcephaly, feeding difficulties, intellectual disability, autistic behavior, kyphosis/scoliosis and camptodactyly/contractures. Two of 3 had cerebral palsy/spasticity, high arched eyebrows, epicanthal folds, a deep/broad nasal bridge, a short/upturned philtrum, low-set ears, widely spaced teeth and hearing impairment. None had hypertelorism, ptosis, strabismus or hernias. The authors noted a large overlap with severe AUTS2 syndrome, but with a wider range and higher rate of congenital malformations.
quotes: Other (camptodactyly/contractures) | 3/3 | -
Kyphosis/scoliosis | 3/3 | 10/47 (21,3%)
A remarkable overlap between the two syndromes was observed with a wider spectrum and higher rate of congenital malformations in children with a pathogenic variant in FBRSL1.

findings.statement: Pauli et al. (2021) noted that all 3 reported patients carried truncating variants in the N-terminal part of FBRSL1 that affect the short N-terminal isoforms: stop variants in 2 patients and a frameshift causing a premature stop codon in 1. By contrast, severe AUTS2 syndrome is linked to variants affecting the AUTS2 C-terminus.
quotes: all three patients harbor a truncating variant (stop mutation in two patients and a frameshift variant with premature stop codon in the other patient) in the N-terminus of FBRSL1 affecting the short N-terminal isoforms

findings.statement: Pauli et al. (2021) summarized Xenopus work in which Fbrsl1 morpholino knockdown caused craniofacial defects with cartilage hypoplasia, smaller brain size, and impaired migration of cranial nerves and motor neurons. A human short N-terminal FBRSL1 isoform rescued the craniofacial defects. Neither a patient-variant version of this isoform nor the long isoform, both lacking the Ftsk domain, rescued them. The authors suggested that mutations in the short N-terminal isoforms cause the developmental phenotype.
quotes: Morpholino-mediated Fbrsl1 knockdown resulted in craniofacial defects and the embryos showed cartilage hypoplasia as well as a reduction in brain size on the injected side (Figures 1A–C).
However, neither a patient variant of this isoform nor the long FBRSL1 isoform, which both lack the Ftsk domain, were able to rescue the morphant phenotype (Ufartes et al., 2020).
These data suggest that mutations of the short N-terminal FBRSL1 isoforms are causative for the developmental phenotype in the animal model system and possibly also in human patients.

findings.statement: Pauli et al. (2021) noted that FBRSL1, like AUTS2, interacts with the Polycomb subcomplexes PRC1.3 and PRC1.5 and competes with AUTS2 for binding to PRC1.5. In HEK293 cells and human fibroblasts, FBRSL1 was found in both the nucleus and the cytoplasm. An N-terminal antibody detected both nuclear and cytoplasmic signal, whereas a C-terminal antibody mainly detected nuclear signal, suggesting that different isoforms have nuclear versus cytoplasmic functions.
quotes: Like AUTS2, FBRSL1 was also identified by tandem affinity purification and mass spectrometry as an interaction partner of PRC1.3 and PRC1.5 (Gao et al., 2012). Further, it was shown that FBRSL1 competes with AUTS2 for binding to the PRC1.5 complex (Gao et al., 2014).
we recently demonstrated that FBRSL1 is localized in the cytoplasm as well as in the nucleus of HEK293 cells and human fibroblasts (Figures 1E,F)

findings.statement: Pauli et al. (2021) described a long 19-exon FBRSL1 transcript (NM_001142641.2) and 2 validated short N-terminal isoforms. The short isoforms use an alternative exon 3 that leads to a stop codon; they lack the AUTS2 family domain but include a predicted DNA translocase (Ftsk) domain.
quotes: Like for AUTS2, a long FBRSL1 transcript containing 19 exons (NM_001142641.2) was identified (Figure 1E) (Ufartes et al., 2020).

The two short isoforms contain an alternative exon three leading to a stop codon. These two short N-terminal forms lack the homologous AUTS2 family domain, but include a predicted DNA translocase domain (Ftsk)

relevance_reason: Original report of de novo truncating FBRSL1 variants in three unrelated children with the syndrome, with functional studies in cells and Xenopus.

findings.statement: Ufartes et al. (2020) reported 3 unrelated children with a recognizable malformation syndrome. All three had impaired intellectual development and/or global developmental delay, delayed speech, autistic behavior, microcephaly, swallowing difficulty, postnatal growth retardation, skeletal abnormalities, camptodactyly/contractures, facial dysmorphism, and respiratory failure that needed ventilation therapy. Heart defects (ASD/PDA, ASD/VSD) were present in 2 patients, as were cleft palate, hearing impairment, and distinctive skin creases. Asplenia and an anal anomaly were each seen in 1 patient.
quotes: All children presented with respiratory insufficiency, feeding difficulties, postnatal growth restriction and microcephaly, global developmental delay, no active speech, contractures, facial dysmorphism and other malformations like heart defects, cleft palate and distinctive skin creases in the first year of life.
Camptodactyly/contractures (HP:0001371) | + | + | + | +
Heart defect (HP:0001627) | ASD/PDA | ASD/VSD | − | Atrial septum defect (ASD)

findings.statement: Ufartes et al. (2020) noted that in 2 of the patients the skin folds were most pronounced right after birth, mainly affected the back rather than the arms and legs, and regressed with age. This pattern differs from congenital symmetric circumferential skin creases syndromes (CSCSC1 and CSCSC2). Other features included a pronounced neck fold, a flat occiput, dysplastic auricles, deep-set eyes, a round face, temporal indentations, contractures of the hands and fingers, and widely spaced teeth.
quotes: The skin phenotype was most pronounced immediately after birth and regressed in both children with increasing age.
the back was preferentially affected in our patients and not the arms and legs
Contractures of both hands and fingers are observed, as well as wide-spaced teeth

findings.statement: Trio exome sequencing by Ufartes et al. (2020) found a heterozygous de novo c.487C>T nonsense variant in FBRSL1 in patient 1, producing p.Gln163*. Sanger sequencing confirmed it, and both unaffected parents carried the wild-type sequence. The variant was absent from gnomAD and ExAC, and the transcript escaped nonsense-mediated decay. Pathogenic variants in TUBB, MAPRE2, and AUTS2 were excluded.
quotes: In patient 1 we identified in a heterozygous state the de novo mutation c.487C > T (12:133,085,942; GRCh37/hg19) in FBRSL1, leading to a premature stop codon (p.Gln163*).
Neither of the three identified variants is listed in the gnomAD database or Exome Aggregation Consortium (ExAC) (Lek et al. 2016).

findings.statement: Ufartes et al. (2020) initially found no change in the canonical FBRSL1 transcript in patient 2. Manual inspection of intronic reads then revealed a heterozygous de novo 23-bp deletion (c.581_603del), which affects alternative exon 3 of the short N-terminal isoform 3.1 (XM_005266181.4). The deletion causes a frameshift and a premature stop at position 356 that disrupts the DNA translocase domain. Sanger sequencing and RT-PCR confirmed it, and both healthy parents were wild type.
quotes: This confirmed a heterozygous state of the 23-bp deletion in the affected child and a wild-type status of this gene region in the healthy parents
The deletion leads to a frameshift with a premature stop codon at position 356 (isoform 3.1), disrupting the DNA translocase domain (amino acid position 444–511, isoform 3.1).

findings.statement: Ufartes et al. (2020) identified a heterozygous c.332G>A nonsense variant in FBRSL1, producing p.Trp111*, in patient 3 by single exome sequencing and reverse phenotyping. The variant was absent from the healthy mother; the father was not available for testing. It was not present in gnomAD or ExAC.
quotes: A third patient with a truncating FBRSL1 mutation (c.332 G > A; p.Trp111*; 12:133,085,787; GRCh37/hg19) was identified by single exome sequencing and reverse phenotyping.
The mutation was not detected in the healthy mother of patient 3. The father was not available for genetic testing.

findings.statement: Using RT-PCR and Western blot, Ufartes et al. (2020) validated short N-terminal FBRSL1 isoforms 3.1 (about 66 kDa) and 3.2 (about 55 kDa) alongside the long isoform 1 (about 110 kDa). The short isoforms contain an FtsK DNA translocase domain, and isoform 1 instead contains an AUTS2 domain. All 3 patient variants affect the short isoforms. Isoform 3.1 was expressed mainly in fetal tissues. N-terminal isoforms localized to the cytoplasm and nucleus and associated with centrosomes and kinetochores.
quotes: Using an N-terminal antibody for Western blot analysis on protein lysates from HEK293 cells we detected an approximately 110 kDa, 66 kDa and 55 kDa band corresponding to the estimated sizes of isoforms 1, 3.1 and 3.2.
In particular, N-terminal FBRSL1 isoforms appeared to be associated with the centrosomes and the kinetochores in dividing cells.
isoform 3.1 showed a clear expression in fetal tissues, with partial lack of expression in the adult tissues

findings.statement: Ufartes et al. (2020) knocked down Fbrsl1 in Xenopus laevis embryos with a splice-blocking morpholino. Knockdown caused reduced craniofacial structures and eyes, cartilage hypoplasia (most severe in the branchial arches), reduced Ncam expression in the brain, and disturbed migration of cranial nerves and motor neurons. Human short isoform 3.1 rescued the craniofacial defects in a dose-dependent manner. Neither the long isoform 1 nor isoform 3.1 carrying p.Gln163* rescued them.
quotes: Interestingly, fbrsl1 MO injection caused a significant reduction of craniofacial structures and the eye in stage 40 Xenopus laevis embryos, whereas wild-type and control MO (co MO) injected embryos developed normally
Co-injection of the FBRSL1 isoform 1 lacking the DNA translocase domain did not rescue the craniofacial defects caused by Fbrsl1 depletion
the mutated human FBRSL1 isoform 3.1-p.Gln163* containing the p.Gln163* mutation from patient 1 also failed to rescue the craniofacial defects caused by Fbrsl1 depletion

findings.statement: Ufartes et al. (2020) noted that the long FBRSL1 isoform appears tolerant to loss of function (pLI = 0.01), so haploinsufficiency of the long transcripts is unlikely. They suggested two possible mechanisms: haploinsufficiency of short isoform 3.2 causing an imbalance between isoforms, or a dominant-negative effect, because the truncated transcripts escaped nonsense-mediated decay.
quotes: Thus, the underlying disease mechanism could be due to haploinsuffiency of the isoform 3.2 and a resulting misbalance between the different FBRSL1 isoforms.
Nevertheless, as truncating alleles of all three patients escaped nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) a dominant-negative mechanism for the detected variants is also conceivable.
